intro: Bali's oldest trees are fig giants kept by temples and villages, spread across the island rather than in one town. Nearest to Ubud is the banyan at Pura Kehen in Bangli, with a drum tower built into its crown. The Kayu Putih tree near Marga is about six metres across at the base, and in the Bedugul highlands the Bali Botanic Garden keeps a fig of eight twisted trunks. In the west a road runs through the base of Bunut Bolong. None has a measured age, so the ages given are local estimates, stated as such.
meta_description: Bali's old fig trees: the Pura Kehen banyan, the Kayu Putih giant, Bunut Bolong and more, where each stands and how to visit.
question_meta: Bali's oldest trees are temple and village figs: the Pura Kehen banyan, the Kayu Putih giant and Bunut Bolong.
question_answer: Bali's best-known old trees are figs kept by temples and villages. The banyan at Pura Kehen in Bangli, about 45 minutes from Ubud, holds a drum tower in its crown and is said to be at least 400 years old. The Kayu Putih tree behind Pura Babakan near Marga, about an hour from Ubud, is about six metres across at the base, and local estimates put it at 500 to 700 years.
question_context: No Indonesian register lists Bali's trees, and none of these has been dated, so every age here is a local or published estimate rather than a measurement. Pura Kehen's figure comes from Wikipedia; the Kayu Putih tree's from a ministry article (more than 500 years) and its caretakers (about 700). The Bali Botanic Garden says its giant fig is more than 100 years old and among its oldest plants. Bunut Bolong in Jembrana, about three hours from Ubud, has no age figure at all, and the Gesing banyan near Munduk rests on travel pages repeating a tradition of 700 years. The species of several is unsettled, so they are entered as Ficus. They are also far apart: Bangli is east of Ubud, Marga and the Bedugul highlands lie north-west, and Bunut Bolong stands on the road from Pekutatan to Singaraja in the far west, so each is a stop by car or scooter. Pura Kehen asks a small donation and a sarong, the Kayu Putih tree takes a donation written in a visitors' book, the botanic garden sells a ticket, and Bunut Bolong stands free beside the public road. Whether the Gesing banyan is open to everyone was not confirmed.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bali?
faq.a: Nobody has dated one. The Kayu Putih tree near Marga in Tabanan carries the highest estimate, 500 to 700 years from a ministry article and its caretakers, and the Pura Kehen banyan in Bangli is said to be at least 400.

faq.q: Which old tree is closest to Ubud?
faq.a: The banyan at Pura Kehen in Bangli, about 45 minutes by car or scooter. The Kayu Putih tree and the Bali Botanic Garden fig are each about an hour away.

faq.q: Can you drive through a tree in Bali?
faq.a: Bunut Bolong in Jembrana has a hole about four metres wide in its base with the road through it, on the route from Pekutatan to Singaraja. By local custom, cremation, wedding and hearse processions take the bypass round it instead.

trees.name: Pura Kehen banyan with the kulkul drum tower

location.address: Pura Kehen, Jalan Sriwijaya, Cempaga, Bangli, Bali

trees.access: Temple open to visitors, small entry donation and sarong required (hours not confirmed from a fetched page). Banyan stands in the outer first courtyard (jaba pisan) just inside the gate; the drum tower in its crown is not climbable by visitors.
trees.transport: No public transport worth the name; about 45 minutes by car or scooter from Ubud (roughly 25 km, via Bangli town).
trees.story:
A wooden drum tower sits in the crown of this banyan, and it was built without stairs. The priest who sounded it reached it through the roots. The tower is a bale kulkul, the slit-drum pavilion a Balinese temple beats to call people in, and here a living tree holds it up. Higher still in the branches sits a monk's cell.

The banyan stands in the outer courtyard of Pura Kehen in Bangli, just past the entrance gate, and the town treats it as sacred. Local belief says a falling branch foretells disaster, which they call grubug, so a broken limb here is read as a warning, not as weather.

How old it is depends on whom you ask. Wikipedia says at least 400 years; the other accounts we found say only centuries old, and nobody has dated the trunk. Take 400 as the one number on offer, not a measurement. The most recent travel and local news pages still describe it standing, but we have no dated photograph, so if you have been lately, tell us.

Our pin marks the temple rather than the tree. Pura Kehen is about 25 km from Ubud, roughly 45 minutes by car or scooter through Bangli town; there is no bus worth waiting for. Expect a small donation at the gate and a sarong to wear inside.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wooden drum pavilion sitting up in its branches. It stands in the first courtyard of Pura Kehen, just inside the entrance gate.

trees.name: Kayu Putih giant tree (Bayan Ancient Tree)

location.address: Behind Pura Babakan, Banjar Bayan, Tua village, Marga, Tabanan, Bali (Google plus code H5VP+9QF)

trees.access: Open daily, entry by voluntary donation written in a visitors' book (no fixed ticket), small parking fee. Stands behind Pura Babakan; no sarong needed to walk round the outside of the tree (per a 2026 visitor guide).
trees.transport: About 1 hour by car or scooter north-west of Ubud (also reachable on the way to Jatiluwih); no public transport. Not a 30-minute trip: label as a day-trip stop.
trees.story:
Nobody can say for certain what kind of tree this is, and its base is about six metres across. Villagers call it kayu putih, white wood, for the pale trunk, or beringin; an article from Indonesia's Ministry of Finance says plainly that the species is not known with certainty. We list it as a fig and would like to be told.

What you see is the root system. Pale buttresses flare out and fold into a sculpted base with a small window straight through the trunk. People have long taken its bark for traditional medicine, and the shrine beside it, Pura Babakan, is named for that bark.

The age is a local estimate either way. The ministry article says more than 500 years. The temple caretakers say about 700, tying it to the age of the village and calling the tree older than Pura Babakan, which they date to the 15th century. Nobody has dated the wood.

Local lore says a gamelan and weapons were buried beneath it in the days of the kingdom, and a neighbour says he has heard gamelan music coming from the tree. It went viral in 2013.

It stands behind Pura Babakan in Banjar Bayan, Tua village, about an hour north-west of Ubud by car or scooter, on the way to Jatiluwih. There is no bus. Entry is a donation written in a visitors' book plus a small parking fee, and you need no sarong to walk round the outside.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the pale buttress roots flaring into a base about six metres across, with a small window through the trunk. It stands behind Pura Babakan in Banjar Bayan.

trees.name: Bunut Bolong

location.address: Jalan Raya Pekutatan to Singaraja, Manggisari, Pekutatan, Jembrana, Bali (Google plus code JV7C+7F)

trees.access: Free, beside the public road between Pekutatan and Singaraja; open 24 hours per the Google listing as relayed by lokasibali. A bypass road runs round the tree; cremation, wedding and hearse traffic is by local custom not allowed through the hole.
trees.transport: About 2 hours by car north-west of Kuta (Bali provincial tourism page), roughly 3 hours from Ubud; a stop on the road to Singaraja. Not a day trip from Ubud cluster; label as a west Bali road-trip stop.
trees.story:
A paved road runs straight through the base of this tree. The hole is nearly four metres wide, and cars drive through a living fig on the road between Pekutatan and Singaraja in west Bali.

Locals call it Bunut Bolong, the hollow bunut, bunut being their name for a banyan-type fig, and also Gelung Kori Agung, the crown of a grand door. The tree stands on a narrow mountain ridge. When the road was cut, the roots were cut with it, but only after ceremonies asking the tree's resident spirits for permission. They are said to be two holy tigers. Prop roots have kept the tree alive since, and it is still widening.

How the hole got there is disputed. One account says it is natural; another says Dutch colonial labourers widened it. Its age is no clearer. The province's tourism page says locals believe it is centuries old, and nobody gives a number. Nor has anyone put a scientific name to it on a page we could read. If you know either, tell us.

The tree still keeps its own traffic rules. By local custom, cremation processions, wedding parties and hearses do not pass through the hole, and take the bypass road round it instead. The neighbouring temple, Pura Bhujangga Sakti, honours the priest Dang Hyang Sidhi Mantra.

It is free and beside a public road, about two hours by car from Kuta and roughly three from Ubud. Treat it as a stop on the drive to Singaraja.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the road running through a hole nearly four metres wide in its base. It stands astride the Pekutatan to Singaraja road at Manggisari, with a bypass road curving round it.

trees.name: Giant Ficus Tree, Bali Botanic Garden

location.address: Bali Botanic Garden (Kebun Raya Eka Karya Bali), Candikuning, Baturiti, Tabanan, Bali, upper slope of Tapak Hill / Rasamala Forest

trees.access: Garden entry ticket (sources disagree: roughly IDR 17,000 to 30,000; Wikipedia infobox 8am-6pm daily, last entry 5.30pm; check kebunraya.id/bali). Walk-in, no tour needed; the tree is inside the garden grounds.
trees.transport: Bedugul highlands, about 1 hour by car or scooter from Ubud (about 50 km north-west); no public transport worth the name. Day-trip stop, not a 30-minute trip.
trees.story:
Eight trunks leave the ground here and twist into a single tree. It is the giant fig of the Bali Botanic Garden, one of the most photographed trees in the garden, and it was here before the garden was.

The garden opened in 1959. Its own page calls the fig more than 100 years old and one of the oldest plants it holds, which puts the tree on this hillside decades before anyone laid out a path to it. How much older is guesswork. A travel writer suggests hundreds of years, and a visitor who logged it in 2013 noted it was believed to be hundreds, but nobody has dated it. The garden's figure is a floor, not a birthday.

The species is open too. Naturalists' records at this spot name it variously as Ficus virens, Ficus altissima or simply Ficus, so we list it as a fig and would welcome a firm answer.

It stands high on the upper slope, which the garden calls the Rasamala Forest and other accounts place on Tapak Hill, with views toward Lake Bratan. Visitors have recorded it standing as recently as October 2026.

The garden sits in the Bedugul highlands, about 50 km north-west of Ubud, roughly an hour by car or scooter; there is no bus worth the name. Entry is a ticket, quoted between about 17,000 and 30,000 rupiah, and the garden keeps daytime hours. Expect an uphill walk once inside.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by eight trunks twisting together into one tree. It stands high on the garden's upper slope, toward Tapak Hill, with views toward Lake Bratan.

trees.name: Gesing giant banyan (near Munduk)

location.address: Jalan Pura Puseh, Gesing village, Banjar, Buleleng, Bali (south of Munduk)

trees.access: Reached by a short track from Gesing, signboards from the village; a guide says visitors can walk among the roots; no entry fee or hours found on any fetched page, one review mentions parking touts and unclear parking fees (Holidify, undated). Kept by the local community as a sacred place (Tatinta). Not confirmed as open to all: ask on the page.
trees.transport: North Bali highlands; about 5 km or 5 to 15 minutes by car from Munduk (sources differ), about 1.5 hours by car from Ubud (balitouristic); no public transport, trekkers walk it from Munduk in roughly an hour (one guide). Day-trip stop.
trees.story:
The roots of this banyan form a maze large enough to walk among, and one account says they once hid villagers from the Dutch. It stands outside Gesing, a village in the north Bali highlands south of Munduk, and the community keeps it as a sacred place. A spirit living in it is said to grant wishes.

Most of what is written about it comes from travel pages that repeat one another, so read every fact here as told rather than checked. Tradition puts the tree at over 700 years. Nobody has dated it, and the same figure is told of the Kayu Putih tree near Marga, so it may have travelled between the two. One page concedes it holds no records for size.

We have no recent dated photograph, and our pin is approximate. Maps show one banyan here and another about 290 metres along the same road, which may be a second tree or the same one marked twice. We found no clear word on entry, fees or hours either, beyond one visitor's complaint about parking touts. If you have stood under it, tell us where it is and what you found there.

A short track leads to it from Gesing, signposted in the village, off Jalan Pura Puseh. Munduk is about 5 km away, 5 to 15 minutes by car depending on the source, and Ubud roughly an hour and a half. There is no bus; trekkers walk it from Munduk in about an hour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the roots, which form arches and passages wide enough to walk among. It stands at the end of a short track from Gesing village, signposted off Jalan Pura Puseh.
